newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Mercedes boss quits in reorganisation row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mercedes boss quits in reorganisation row.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz chairman Helmut Werner, the architect of the biggest shift in strategy in the car maker's history, resigned on Thursday following a bitter struggle over the restructuring of parent Daimler-Benz AG .

Werner, who had opposed plans that legally wind up Mercedes and make it part of Daimler, offered his resignation to Daimler's four-man presidium, which was meeting to hash out details of the overhaul.

Daimler officials, who had hoped the highly respected Werner would remain in the restructured group, said the Mercedes boss approved of the reorganisation plans, but in the end saw no room for his experience in the new organisation.
"The offers for assumption of new responsibilities within the Daimler-Benz board did not fulfil the requirements which he himself put forward," the Daimler statement said.

According to the restructuring plans, Mercedes will cease to be an independent legal entity and will become part of Daimler-Benz, represented on the board by three executives, one for cars, one for trucks and one for marketing.
The Daimler supervisory board is scheduled to meet on January 23 to formally approve the restructuring plans.
Although both men strongly denied it, the German media has been rife with talk of a power struggle between Daimler-Benz AG chairman Schrempp and Werner for months.

Werner, whose unit accounted for 70 percent of Daimler's sales and nearly all its profits, strongly believed that the company should remain fully independent and was thought to resent interference from group management.

Company sources said they hope the restructuring, which is expected to leave Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and Debis AG as full legal entities, will speed up decision-making and cut out layers of middle managmement.

Daimler first began considering a restructuring about a year ago when it became evident that the holding company structure put into place in 1988 was not suited to a business that increasingly was dependent on Mercedes.

Werner, who became Mercedes chairman in May 1993, presided over a contoversial broadening of Mercedes product line. It saw the carmaker, which had long had a "country club" image, move into smaller cars such as the two-seat A-class and the fast-selling SLK roadster sports car.
In his six years at the helm, he took the company from an 800 million mark loss to a net profit of 2.275 billion marks ($1.43 billion), making Mercedes one of the world's most profitable carmakers.

Although some analysts thought Werner was risking the Mercedes' image by moving "down market", he contended the changes were needed to help improve sales which had been growing only slowly among the carmaker's traditional markets.

The Mercedes chairman was also a leading spokesman for the German car industry as a whole, championing efforts to make the workforce more competitive and calling on the government to repeal a controversial tax on company cars.

Werner, famous for his competitive nature which included out-of-office pursuits such as skiing, swiming and tennis, had aimed to double Mercedes production to 1.2 million units within five years, near the same unit sales as arch-rival BMW AG.
Werner has spent most of his career in the industry and had been chairman of tyre maker Continental AG between January 1982 and 1987 when he joined Daimler-Benz.
Analysts said the Werner's departure should not mark a significant change in Mercede's strategy even though Schrempp now stands to play a greater role in the car business.
"The strategy had already been pretty well sketched out," one London-based analyst said. ($1=1.5934 Mark)
